title: Chapter 36: The Stalk of Grass 4
content:
Chapter 36

Jin Ling and the others felt their hearts pounding in their throats, terrified that whatever lurked outside would blindside Wei Wuxian—leaving him clutching his eyes and collapsing to the floorboards. So when Wei Wuxian suddenly gasped out an “Ah!”, every boy’s heart leaped straight into his chest, the hair on their arms standing on end.

"What happened?!" they whispered frantically.

Wei Wuxian hushed them in an impossibly quiet murmur. "Shh! Keep it down. I’m looking at it."

Jin Ling dialed his voice even lower than Wei Wuxian’s. "What do you see? What’s out there?"

Wei Wuxian didn’t peel his eye from the seam, nor did he give a straight answer. "Mm-hmm... Oh, wow... Incredible. Truly incredible."

The profile of his face was painted with pure delight; his awe and wonder sounded completely unfeigned, instantly stoking the young cultivators' curiosity until it easily overwhelmed their dread. Lan Sizhui couldn't stop himself from leaning in. "...Senior Mo, what’s so incredible?"

"My word!" Wei Wuxian breathed. "It's gorgeous. Keep your voices down, don't scare it off—I haven't had my fill yet."

Jin Ling bristled. "Move! Let me look."

"Me too!" another boy chimed in.

Wei Wuxian hesitated, glancing back. "You really want to see?"

"Yes!"

Moving at a snail's pace, Wei Wuxian stepped aside with palpable reluctance. Jin Ling was the first to shove his way forward, pressing his eye right against the sliver of space between the boards to peer outside.

Night had fully fallen. With the cold creeping in, the unnatural fog cloaking Yi City had thinned considerably, allowing a faint view of the street several yards out. Jin Ling squinted into the gloom for a while, but caught no glimpse of this "incredible, gorgeous" marvel. Disappointment prickled through him.Did my voice scare it away just now?

Just as he was about to write it off as a dud, a shriveled, emaciated silhouette flashed right into his field of vision.

Taking in the thing's full, ghastly visage point-blank without an ounce of warning nearly blew Jin Ling's scalp clean off. A shriek climbed straight into his throat, but through sheer stubborn pride, he swallowed the yell whole, choking it back down. Pinned in an awkward, bent-over crouch, he waited for the prickling numbness across his scalp to subside before whipping his head around to glare at Wei Wuxian.

The insufferable man was leaning against the shutter, a smug smirk tugging at one corner of his mouth as he arched a brow. "Well?" Wei Wuxian drawled with a sly grin. "Isn't it a looker?"

Jin Ling shot him a murderous glare, knowing full well he’d been played. He ground his teeth together. "...Stunning."

A wicked thought sparked in his mind. Straightening up, Jin Ling feigned utter indifference. "Nothing special, honestly. Barely worth a glance!"

He stepped aside with a casual shrug, waiting for the next sucker to take the bait. With the two of them putting on such a seamless performance, the rest of the boys were practically dying of curiosity. Unable to resist, Lan Sizhui stepped up to take the spot.

The second he pressed his eye to the crack, however, he let out a painfully honest, strangled yelp and scrambled backward, his face drained of color. Dazed and spinning around twice before locating Wei Wuxian, he pointed an accusing finger. "Senior Mo! Outside, there's... there's..."

Wei Wuxian nodded knowingly. "There'sthat, right? Don't spoil it! It ruins the surprise. Let the others look for themselves."

Watching Sizhui get rattled to his core was enough to make the others balk; surprise, my foot—it was pure nightmare fuel! They waved their hands frantically. "No way, we're not looking!"

Jin Ling scoffed, "Playing pranks at a time like this... I swear, I have no idea what goes on in that head of yours!"

"Didn't you help set the trap?" Wei Wuxian fired back. "And drop the attitude; you're starting to sound just like your uncle. Sizhui, was it scary?"

Sizhui nodded, answering honestly, "Terrifying."

"Good, that's the point," Wei Wuxian said. "This is prime training material. Why do ghosts try to terrify people? Because the moment you're scared out of your wits, your mental defenses shatter and your spiritual essence flares up—that's when it's easiest for them to drain your yang energy. That means what ghosts fear most are bold people. A fearless person gives them nothing to work with; they're out of options. So, as disciples of noble clans, your very first duty is to thicken your hide and grow some nerve!"

Lan Jingyi, internally praising the heavens that he was temporarily paralyzed and hadn't stepped up to look, grumbled from the sidelines, "Courage is born, not made. What are you supposed to do if you're just naturally jumpy?"

"Were you born knowing how to fly on a sword?" Wei Wuxian retorted. "You practiced until it became second nature. Fear works the exact same way—get scared enough times, and you get numb to it. Latrines stink, right? Disgusting, right? But take my word for it: live in an outhouse for a month, and you'll be happily shoveling rice down your throat in there."

A chorus of horrified groans swept the room. "No way in hell! We don't believe you!"

"It was just an analogy," Wei Wuxian conceded. "Fine, I admit it: I've never lived in a latrine, I don't know if I could stomach eating there, and I'm talking out of my ass. But the thing outside? You absolutely need to face it. Don't just peek—study it. Note its features, and dig through the details to pinpoint its potential weaknesses in the shortest time possible. Stay calm under pressure and find your opening to strike back. Now, after all that lecturing, did any of it sink in? It's not every day you get guidance like this, so treasure it. Stop shrinking back—form a line, one by one."

"...Do we really have to?" a voice whimpered.

"Naturally," Wei Wuxian declared. "I never joke, and I certainly never mess with people. Let's start with Jingyi. Jin Ling and Sizhui have already had their turn."

Jingyi stammered, "Huh? I get a pass, right? You said it yourself—anyone with corpse poisoning shouldn't move!"

Wei Wuxian walked over. "Stick your tongue out. Say 'ah.'"

"Ah."

Wei Wuxian beamed. "Congratulations, the toxin's cleared! Take that brave first step—chop chop!"

Jingyi was flabbergasted. "It cleared already?! You're pulling my leg!"

With his protest dead in the water, he had no choice but to drag his feet to the window, taking quick, terrified peeks before violently jerking his head away.

Wei Wuxian rapped a knuckle against the wood. "What are you sweating over? I'm standing right here. It wouldn't dare breach this plank, and it's not going to pluck your eyeballs out."

Jingyi leaped back. "Done! I looked!"

One by one, the rest of the boys stepped up, each letting out sharp, hissing gasps of breath as they took their turn. Once the rotation finished, Wei Wuxian crossed his arms. "Seen enough? Alright, everyone call out the details you caught. Let's break it down."

Jin Ling jumped in first. "Milky white pupils. Female. Short and scrawny. Decent-looking. Carrying a bamboo pole."

Sizhui pondered for a beat before adding, "She reaches about my chest. Her clothes are tattered and soiled, resembling a street beggar's garb. That bamboo stick looks like a blind cane; those white pupils might not have formed after death, meaning she was likely blind while alive."

Wei Wuxian nodded in evaluation. "Jin Ling caught the broad strokes, but Sizhui caught the nuances."

Jin Ling merely clicked his tongue.

Another disciple spoke up: "She looks about fifteen or sixteen, with an oval face—quite delicate, but with a lively edge to her. Her hair is pinned up with a wooden hairpin carved like a little fox head at the end. She's thin and slight of frame. Disheveled, sure, but not filthy or repulsive. Cleaned up, she'd honestly be a pretty girl."

Wei Wuxian’s eyes lit up, thoroughly impressed by the boy's sharp eye. "Not bad at all! Meticulous observation with a very unique focal point. Mark my words, this kid is going to be quite the romantic."

The boy's face flushed scarlet, and he buried his head against the wall to dodge his peers' teasing snickers.

Another disciple chimed in, "So that tapping sound was just her cane hitting the pavement. If she was blind in life, her ghost would remain sightless; she'd have to rely on that stick to navigate."

"Wait, that doesn't add up," another boy argued. "You've all seen blind folk before, right? Lacking sight, they move slowly and gingerly, terrified of bumping into things. But that ghost outside was fast on her feet. I've never seen a blind person move with that kind of agility."

Wei Wuxian smiled warmly. "Catching that discrepancy—very good. That's exactly how you should dissect a mystery: leave no loose thread unpulled. Well then, let's invite her in and get our answers straight from the source."

Before anyone could process his words, he tore a plank clean off the doorframe. The sudden move spooked not just the disciples inside, but the ghost lingering on the other side, who raised her bamboo cane in defensive alarm.

Wei Wuxian offered a polite nod of greeting before asking, "Young lady, you've been dogging their steps for a while now. Is there something you need?"

The girl’s eyes went wide. On a living maiden, the expression would have been downright charming, but framed by pupilless white eyes spilling twin tracks of bloody tears, it looked thoroughly ghastly. A few gasps broke out behind him, prompting Wei Wuxian to sigh, "What's there to flinch at? You'll see plenty of corpses bleeding from all seven apertures down the line; crying blood from two is already giving you the gentle treatment. That's why you need the field experience."

The ghost, who had spent the last hour pacing frantically outside, stamping her feet and waving her arms, suddenly shifted her movements. She began gesturing rapidly, desperate to convey a message.

Jin Ling frowned. "Strange. Can't she speak?"

At his words, the girl froze, then opened her mouth wide.

Fresh blood spilled from the hollow cavern behind her lips. Her tongue had been torn out by the roots.

A collective chill ran down the boys' spines, quickly giving way to a shared pang of sympathy.No wonder she's mute. Blind and robbed of speech—how miserable.

Wei Wuxian asked, "Is that sign language? Does anyone read it?"

Nobody did. The girl stamped her feet in sheer frustration, dropping to the dirt to scratch out shapes with her cane. But having clearly never had the luxury of schooling, she was illiterate and couldn't write a single word. The chaotic mess of stick figures she scratched out was completely indecipherable.

Right then, the sound of hurried footsteps and ragged panting broke through the silence of the far street.

The girl's spirit vanished on the spot, but knowing she'd find her way back, Wei Wuxian didn't fret. He jammed the wooden board back into place, peering out through the crack once more. The other disciples clamored behind him, stacking their heads from top to bottom like a totem pole just to catch a glimpse of the street.

The fog that had cleared earlier was beginning to churn back into thick waves. A battered figure tore through the white haze, stumbling down the lane.

He was clad in black robes, looking injured as he limped forward, a sword wrapped in dark cloth hanging from his sash.

Lan Jingyi whispered, "Is that the fog-masked guy from earlier?"

"Doubtful," Sizhui murmured back. "His footwork is entirely different."

A horde of walking corpses surged through the mist, their unnerving speed closing the distance in seconds. The swordsman drew his blade to meet them, the pristine, crystalline light of his steel slicing clean through the gloom. Wei Wuxian silently praised the strike:What a magnificent sword!

Yet with that sweep came that familiar, sickening splutter. Blackish-red powder erupted from the severed limbs of the corpses. Hemmed in on all sides, the swordsman had nowhere to dodge, catching the cloud of toxic dust full in the face.

Sizhui watched with growing dread. "Senior Mo, should we..."

Before he could finish, another wave of corpses swarmed the man, tightening the noose. Another sword stroke unleashed a fresh plume of powder, and having inhaled too much of the grit, the swordsman began to sway on his feet.

Wei Wuxian’s tone sharpened. "We need to pull him out."

"How are we supposed to do that?" Jin Ling challenged. "We can't go out there—the air is choked with corpse powder. Step outside and you're poisoned!"

After a heartbeat's calculation, Wei Wuxian turned away from the window and strode into the center of the hall, the disciples' gazes tracking him in confusion. Standing silently between the two massive funerary wreaths was the crowd of paper mortuary figures. Wei Wuxian strolled past them, coming to a halt before a particular pair of paper maidens.

While the other figures varied in design, these two were clearly crafted as twin sisters—their features, makeup, and attire practically identical, their smiling faces and curved eyes looking as though they were about to burst into giggles. Their hair was styled in double loops, adorned with red bead earrings, gold bracelets painted on their paper wrists, and delicate embroidered slippers at their feet—the spitting image of pampered maidservants from an aristocratic estate.

"You two will do," Wei Wuxian decided.

Catching the bare blade of a disciple's drawn sword, he dragged his thumb across the edge, slicing open a shallow cut. Wheeling around, he dabbed four dots of fresh blood onto the figures, painting pupils onto their stark white eyes.

Stepping back with a faint, knowing smile, he chanted softly:

"Languid eyes half-closed in grace,

Ruby lips that softly tease.

Ask no question of their heart,

Bring the paper soul to life."

An unnatural, freezing draft howled out of nowhere, filling the shop with a bone-deep chill. The disciples instinctively tightened their grips on their hilts.

Suddenly, the twin paper maidens shuddered violently.

The very next second, sweet, lilting giggles drifted out from behind their painted crimson lips!

Paper Puppet Invocation!

As though privy to the funniest joke in the world, the paper maidens shook with helpless laughter, their blood-painted pupils rolling wildly within paper sockets—a sight as sickeningly charming as it was utterly horrifying. Wei Wuxian offered them a shallow nod, bowing from the waist.

Returning the courtesy, the paper twins dipped into a deep, sweeping curtsy.

Wei Wuxian pointed toward the entrance. "Bring the living man inside. Everything else—annihilate without mercy."

High, piercing laughter tore from their mouths as a violent gust of wind kicked the heavy doors wide!

The paper twins shot through the opening shoulder-to-shoulder, diving straight into the swarm of corpses. It was surreal to witness; though forged from fragile paper, their killing power was downright monstrous. Gliding gracefully on paper slippers, the flutter of their billowing sleeves sheared through corpse arms like iron cleavers, a backhand sweep lopping off skulls in neat halves, their paper hems harder than tempered steel. That delicate, eerie laughter echoed down the empty avenue, a sound both mesmerizing and deeply unnerving.

Within moments, over a dozen walking corpses were reduced to a scattered mess of unrecognizable limbs littering the cobblestones!

Having claimed absolute victory, the maidservants dutifully hauled the flagging swordsman over the threshold before hopping back out onto the street, the heavy doors snapping shut behind them. Flanking the entrance like stone guard lions, they fell dead silent.

Inside, the young cultivators stood paralyzed, jaws hanging slack.

Growing up on orthodox scriptures, they’d only ever heard crooked cultivation described by their elders, leaving them endlessly puzzled:If these methods are so vile, why are so many people desperate to learn them? Why does the Yiling Laozu still command such an army of imitators?Seeing it with their own eyes, however, the sheer, intoxicating wonder of the craft became brutally clear. And this was merely the tip of the iceberg—the Paper Puppet Invocation. Far from feeling revulsion, most of the boys shook off their shock only to wear looks of uncontainable excitement, already daydreaming about how they’d brag to their peers back home.

Only Jin Ling’s face remained as black as thunder.

Lan Sizhui stepped forward to help prop the man up, but Wei Wuxian held up a warning hand. "Stay back, all of you. Don't touch that corpse powder—it might seep straight through bare skin."

The man had been drifting in and out of consciousness when the paper dolls dragged him inside. Stirring slightly, he coughed into his sleeve, carefully muffling his mouth so as not to spray the toxic powder over anyone else. "Who... who are you?" he rasped, his voice dripping with exhaustion.

The question wasn't just born of unfamiliarity; it was because he couldn't see a thing.

Thick layers of white gauze were wrapped around his eyes. He was blind.

Worse, he was an exceptionally handsome blind man—a straight, elegant nose and pale, soft lips that gave him a youthful, refined grace, sitting somewhere between a youth and a grown man. It was the sort of visage that made you mourn the tragedy of his lost sight.

Wei Wuxian mused darkly to himself:What is with this town? Blind people everywhere—tales of them, sights of them. Living ones, dead ones.

Jin Ling broke the silence, his tone sharp. "Hey. We don't even know who this guy is, or whether he's friend or foe. Why rescue him on a whim? If he turns out to be a villain, we just brought a viper into the house!"

The logic was sound, but airing it so bluntly in front of the man was painfully awkward. Yet the stranger didn't take offense, nor did he look perturbed about being tossed back onto the street. Instead, a faint smile graced his lips, flashing a pair of small, sharp canine teeth. "The young gentleman makes a fair point. It would be better if I took my leave."

Jin Ling hadn't anticipated such a gentle surrender and froze, caught flat-footed, managing only a clumsy grunt.

Sizhui hastily smoothed things over. "He might just as easily be an upright gentleman! Leaving someone to die goes against our clan's core principles anyway."

Jin Ling dug his heels in. "Fine! You're all saints. Just don't come crying to me if someone loses an arm!"

"You really are impossible..." Lan Jingyi started, only for his tongue to twist into knots.

His eyes had snagged on the sword propped against the table. The dark cloth wrapped around the scabbard had slipped loose, exposing a length of the weapon.

The craftsmanship was sublime. The scabbard was forged from antique bronze, intricately carved with openwork frost-flower filigree. Peeking through the cutouts, the blade caught the light like polished silver, shimmering with delicate snowflake-shaped gleams—an aura of pure, pristine elegance and dazzling brilliance.

Jingyi’s eyes went wide, words ready to spill from his lips. Though Wei Wuxian didn't know what name was about to be shouted, the cloth wrap made it obvious the wielder wanted the blade hidden; unwilling to stir up trouble, Wei Wuxian clamped a hand over Jingyi’s mouth, pressing an index finger to his own lips to hush the rest of the wide-eyed boys.

Jin Ling silently mouthed two characters, then reached out to trace them into the dust on the tabletop:

Shuanghua.

...The sword Shuanghua?

Wei Wuxian mouthed back silently:Xiao Xingchen’s Shuanghua?

Jin Ling and the disciples nodded in unison.

None of the boys had ever met Xiao Xingchen in the flesh, but Shuanghua was legendary—renowned not just for its vast spiritual reservoir, but for its exquisite design, immortalized across countless compendiums of sacred blades. Wei Wuxian’s brow furrowed.If that blade is Shuanghua, and the wielder is blind...

Another disciple, arriving at the exact same conclusion, impulsively reached out toward the linen wrapped around the man's face, itching to see whether the eyes beneath were truly gone. But the instant his fingertips brushed the fabric, the stranger's face twisted in sheer agony, flinching back with an instinctive, terrified shudder.

Catching his own blunder, the boy snatched his hand back. "I'm sorry, I'm so sorry! I didn't mean to!"

The man raised his left hand—clad in a thin black glove—hovering his fingers over the bandages as if to shield them, yet not daring to touch the cloth. A light bead of sweat broke out across his brow, the sheer agony of a glancing brush clearly unbearable. He forced a strained whisper: "It's... it's fine..."

His voice trembled slightly.

That reaction settled it: this man was almost certainly Xiao Xingchen, who had vanished without a trace following the tragedy of the Yueyang Chang Clan.

Oblivious that his identity had been blown, the man rode out the wave of pain before blindly groping for his sword. Wei Wuxian swiftly smoothed the dark cloth back over the exposed steel. Fingers wrapping around the hilt, the man offered a faint nod. "My thanks for the rescue. I shall take my leave."

Wei Wuxian caught his sleeve. "Don't go just yet. You've been hit with corpse poisoning."

"Is it severe?" the man asked.

"Extremely," Wei Wuxian said.

"If it is truly that severe, what point is there in lingering?" the man reasoned softly. "Since I am beyond saving, I might as well put down a few more walking corpses before the transformation takes me."

Hearing him discard his own life so casually set the boys' blood boiling with righteous indignation. Lan Jingyi blurted out, "Who says you're beyond saving?! Stay put! He'll fix you up!"

Wei Wuxian’s eye twitched.Me? Excuse me, are you talking about me?He didn't have the heart to drop the hammer: this "Xiao Xingchen" had inhaled far too much corpse dust, his complexion already tinged with an ominous purplish-black. The venom ran so deep that a bowl of glutinous rice congee wouldn't do a damn thing.

The blind cultivator continued, "I have put down many corpses in this city; they have been hunting me, and more will follow shortly. If I stay, this place will eventually be overrun."

Wei Wuxian asked, "Do you have any idea how Yi City ended up in this state?"

The man shook his head. "I do not. I am merely a wandering Dao... a wandering cultivator passing through. Catching wind of the anomalies here, I entered to night-hunt. You have yet to witness the sheer number and ferocity of the dead stalking these lanes. Some move with blinding speed, impossible to predict. Others vent plumes of lethal corpse dust upon falling—touch it and you are poisoned, yet leave them unchecked and they will tear you to pieces, yielding the exact same fate. They are dreadfully difficult to manage. Judging by your voices, many of you are young masters of noble houses. I urge you all to depart while you still can."

Right as the words left his mouth, the paper twins outside erupted into sharp, sinister giggles.

This time, the laughter was piercing enough to rattle the glass.
